speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Built Environment sector, especially the construction industry has been severely impacted by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Almost all construction work stopped during the circuit breaker period last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Many companies, particularly our SMEs were hard hit as no work meant there was no progress payment.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Even when works restarted, companies had to adapt to new requirements, such as ensuring our workers attend their rostered routine testing and adhering to safe management measures at the worksites.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In response, the Government has intervened very significantly to support the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The most recent measures announced last week include the waivers for foreign worker levies for construction Work Permit and S Pass holders during their SHN period of 14 to 21 days upon entry into Singapore, for the period between 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have also put in place legislation through the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act to provide temporary relief to businesses and individuals who are unable to perform their contractual obligations due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This ensured that no one single part of the built environment value chain has to bear a disproportionate share of the burden brought about by the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: To recap, Part 2 of the Act provides temporary relief from stipulated types of legal actions and also provides firms with a defence against breach of contract and damages due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Under Part 8, we provided a mechanism for firms to seek relief from additional rental costs that are incurred due to construction delays caused by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Under Part 8B, we required the players in the value chain, from builders to contractors to sub-contractors to co-share additional costs for delays also due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Under Part 8C, developers who face construction delay can seek relief on the date of delivery of possession.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We also provided for the co-sharing between developers and purchasers of the out-of-pocket costs incurred by purchasers where developers are not able to deliver the units by the committed delivery date due to delays caused by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We are working closely with industry partners to get the sector to get back on its feet.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: I am pleased to share that almost all our construction S Pass and work permit holders have returned to work, although the numbers have decreased by about 15% in January 2021 compared to the year before.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The last infection case for construction S Pass and work permit holders in our dormitories was more than 30 days ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Construction activities at the worksites have largely resumed, to approximately 85% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Construction demand is expected to rebound to some extent in the next few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, despite this steady progress, firms in the built environment sector continue to face significant pressures in the near term.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Construction projects have to manage with lower productivity on site due to safe management measures, which are needed to keep our workers and the broader community safe.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Firms face shortages of manpower and labour cost increases as we need to continue to limit the inflow of migrant workers into Singapore for good public health reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: BCA and MOH are reviewing the safe management measures at worksites, taking into account the need to balance the risk of on-site transmission and other considerations including the vaccination of our migrant worker population.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have commenced COVID-19 vaccination for migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: To date, 97% of some 9,000 COVID-19-naïve workers from five largest dormitories have received their first dose of vaccine.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: A further 30,000 migrant workers across 30 dorms are scheduled to get their first dose in the coming weeks.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The take-up of the vaccination has been encouraging and we aim to make significant progress by the end of the year, in lockstep with the nation’s vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Therefore, Mr Speaker, Sir, while the sector is slowly getting back on its feet, we are not out of the woods yet.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It is in this context that I am introducing the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 2) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: First, the proposed amendments to the Act will allow us to extend the existing reliefs for the sector provided under Part 2 of the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will have the effect of extending the period for cost-sharing in construction contracts under Part 8B of the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Second, the proposed amendments will also allow us to better administer Part 8C of the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The construction industry has long and complex value chains, with multiple tiers of sub-contracting.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Given the cascading chain nature of construction and supply contracts across the multiple tiers, an expiry of the relief could result in a wave of contractual disputes, especially during this time when the sector is still stabilising.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: If firms embroiled in legal disputes are forced to wind up, this could lead to a domino effect where multiple firms along the value chain would wind up successively.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Contractors who incur additional cost as a result of COVID-19 would also benefit from this extension.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, the cost-sharing under Part 8B will still remain at 50% of the qualifying costs and will still be subject to a monthly cap of 0.2% of contract sum per month, and a total 1.8% of the contract sum.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will provide more time for developers and purchasers who are unable to perform any of their contractual obligations to negotiate and reach a compromise.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In particular, in view of the impact of the COVID-19 situation on the economy, it will assist purchasers who require more time to sort out their finances and make their payments.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill will amend the sunset period under Part 2 of the Act, so that the reliefs under that part can subsist beyond the sunset date of 19 April 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will allow for the extension of the relief periods for construction and supply contracts, options to purchase, and agreements for the sale and purchase of properties beyond the current sunset date of 19 April 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Next, this Bill also introduces a number of amendments to Part 8C of the Act to facilitate the implementation and the delivery of the relief when it comes into operation in a few months.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have been working very closely with the relevant agencies and industry stakeholders on the operational details.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We want to ensure that the process of tapping on the relief is efficient for both the purchasers and the developers, given that this will be in effect for a longer period as compared to the other reliefs under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Part 8C is intended to assist developers who are facing construction delay due to COVID-19 and are unable to meet the committed delivery date of possession to purchasers.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have been encouraging developers who are unable to meet the date of delivery of possession to first discuss with their purchasers and come to a workable and mutually agreeable arrangement.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Should the developer need relief of more than 122 days, they can apply to an assessor for a determination of the length of construction delay that is caused by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And where the developer has extended the date of delivery of possession, purchasers may seek reimbursement from the developer for certain out-of-pocket expenses incurred due to the delay in delivery of the unit, up to a specified cap.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This allows for co-sharing of such costs between the developer and the purchaser and if there are any disputes, parties can apply to an assessor for a determination.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The assessor will consider the facts of the matter and make a fair and just determination of the cost that the purchaser is entitled to claim from the developer.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 4 amends the Act to provide for the different manners in which the purchaser may claim and obtain reimbursement of qualifying costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, after the amount has been determined, the developer can directly reimburse the purchaser, or the purchaser can offset the amount of reimbursement against any instalment or other payment payable by the purchaser to the developer under the affected agreement.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will provide more options for purchasers and developers to settle between themselves the reimbursement that is due based on what works best for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 5 introduces a new provision to empower the Registrar of assessors to, on such terms as a Registrar of assessor thinks just, extend the period within which a person is required under Part 8C to do anything.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: There may be instances where parties have genuine exceptional circumstances for requiring more time to carry out an action in relation to the relief.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And this provision gives the Registrar the flexibility to extend the time for these parties, if the extension is justified.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 6 amends the Act to provide that the Minister is to appoint one or more authorised nominating bodies for the purpose of providing assessors to hear and determine applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As Part 8C will be operational for a few years until the projects of all qualifying current contracts are completed, we can expect personnel changes amongst the assessors.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Allowing the authorised nominating bodies the point assessors who satisfy the requirements prescribed will facilitate a more efficient management of personnel turnover.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clauses 8 and 9 deal with miscellaneous matters relating to proceedings before an assessor, including subsequent determinations and the confidentiality of information and documents, and the making of regulations under this part.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Built Environment sector builds our homes and workplaces, lays our essential infrastructure, like roads and utilities and develops our recreational and green spaces like malls and parks.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: An impact to the Built Environment sector goes beyond the stakeholders in the value chain and will affect other industries and Singaporeans in one way or another.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: With that, Mr Speaker Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I spoke to a number of players in the industry and they voice appreciation for the Government's COVID-19 related support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These include controlling the pandemic despite all odds, reducing foreign workers levy during the height of COVID-19, pushing forward additional Government support projects, getting banks to provide much-needed support, proceeding to pay for some Government projects, even as constructions were delayed, and to this Bill today pushing for moratorium in legal actions arising from the delay.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The recent announcement to remove foreign workers levy during quarantine is also very welcomed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Nevertheless, COVID-19 represents a big and complex crises for the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This can be seen in the escalating costs of successful BTO construction tender bids from pre-COVID-19 days to today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The surging of manpower cost is, in turn, largely due to three factors: the cost of Safe Management Measures (SMMs), high attrition of assisting migrant workers and difficulty to safely bring in adequate replacement of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: First, the cost of SMMs is unavoidable because it is the price of keeping COVID-19 under control.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, we are seeing higher worker attrition because many workers want to return home to be there for the family during COVID-19, while some workers went back, but could not return.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And some industry players also worried that after vaccination, some of our workers may leave Singapore and seek what they believe is greener pastures, given the widespread migrant worker shortage in other advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Due to this higher natural attrition, a number of migrant workers, especially those in smaller firms, have asked for hefty pay increases in return for staying on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: MOM has recently limited the number of workers that companies can poach from one another and this has reduced the pressure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But the real solution is to ensure the safe replacement of sufficient number of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And so that brings me to my third point, the challenge of bringing in replacement workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Despite the COVID-19 insurance, many firms fear the potential extra medical costs in a range of tens of thousands of dollars should any of the incoming workers suffer from severe COVID-19 symptoms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, while large companies working on projects of healthy margins and has the financial muscle and the cash flow to absorb this cost in the short run, we need to urgently resolve the safe replacement to help the rest of the industry along.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: After discussing with some industry players, I would like to propose this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, can we run commercial processing centres in those cities that will give us full operational control to ensure that testing is done by vetted vendors?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The workers who have passed the test or who have already acquired immunity can be immediately transported to Singapore safely.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And once they arrive in Singapore, they can be immediately get tested and vaccinated during quarantine.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: COVID-19 has brought upon an existentialist threat to the Built Environment sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Decisive and effective Government action has put off the worst outcome for the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Moving forward, the Built Environment sector is grappling with surging costs, which means higher construction costs for Singapore, diminishing margins for most part of the industry and increased risk of project delays and chain bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even as we push for the Built Environment sector to achieve higher manpower productivity in the long run, it is necessary for us to do more to bring an adequate replacement migrant workers in the immediate future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And this will ensure that as much of the recent construction cost surge is transient rather than permanent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These parts were enacted to enable parties to apply for temporary relief from fulfilling contractual obligations affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The proposed extension is a recognition of the ground reality that there are still many businesses and individuals which continue to suffer adverse impacts from COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that the Government has decided, however, not to extend Part 3, which provides for temporary relief for financially distressed individuals and entities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet today, we still see individuals and businesses who are drastically affected by the COVID-19 restrictions from earning income to pay their bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include our residents who used to run excursion and catering businesses, who have so far been unable to pivot to other business models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we inch towards economic recovery, COVID-19 support programmes are being scaled down or stopped.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, economic recovery has been uneven across sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move to the amendments to Part 8C of the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Part 8C deals with the extension of the delivery date of property under sale and purchase agreements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It enables developers, HDB and JTC to have more time to complete construction projects delayed by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also enables purchasers of units to claim additional costs incurred by the delays such as the cost of alternative accommodation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Part 8C was enacted into law by Parliament in November last year under the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From what I understand, Part C has not come into operation yet and I believe earlier the Minister of State did say it would be operational in a few months' time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder why this is so since the amendments in November last year were brought to the House on a Certificate of Urgency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In comparison, the amendments relating to TraceTogether were brought to Parliament only in February this year and are already in force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, could the Minister explain why the amendments to Part 8C are being made even before the provisions become operational?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I recall that at the November sitting, the Minister had assured Members that those provisions were drafted after wide consultations with the industry and were supported by the industry associations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I wish to make two observations about clause 8 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I particularly welcome the new Section 39 OA, which provides for subsequent determination by an assessor based on new information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an important avenue to correct any injustice caused by an original determination, which was later proved to be unwise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 8 also introduces a new section 39 OB which provides that parties coming for an assessment cannot be represented an advocate and solicitor unless special permission is given.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a "no-lawyers-allowed" clause is not novel and is present in other legislation that aimed to provide low cost and less formal dispute resolution mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Despite the good intention behind this no-lawyers-allowed rule, I wish to point out that experience has shown that this can inadvertently lead to unfairness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Residents who have gone through such hearings have highlighted to me that parties who are corporations have the advantage of sending their legally trained employees to represent the corporate entity, thus somewhat circumventing the no-lawyers-allowed rule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has happened in the Employment Claims Tribunal and before the Financial Industry Dispute Resolution Centre or FIDReC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Corporate employers and financial institutions send their in-house counsel, who are not considered advocates and solicitors, while the employee or bank customer has to appear in his own capacity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This imbalance of knowledge and power has the potential to lead to an unjust outcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For this Bill, it is foreseeable that developers, HDB and JTC will send legally trained employees to present their cases in front of assessors, while the purchaser has to prepare his own case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Labour supply has been constrained, and cashflow has been tight.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some construction firms have already gone under, and the struggle is real for those still clinging on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those who have to pay will have more time to pay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those who need to deliver will have more time to deliver.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about what factors that went into deciding on this extension.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But a strong economic recovery must also be built on the rock-solid foundation of contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I support these amendments, can I ask if MND has also studied the impacts to the companies the construction firms has been granted relief from?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are these companies also clinging on and will they go under due to these reliefs granted to the construction firms?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have said that during this relief period, parties are encouraged to negotiate and resolve their difference in an amicable and mutually beneficial manner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask Minister what percentage of parties were able to resolve their difference in an amicable and mutually beneficial manner?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, I hope that MND can help shed light on a few questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can MND share what factors it considered in determining this particular course of action?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can MND share whether it will consider future extensions of the same nature and, if so, what factors it will consider before making such decisions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we should also be concerned about the unintended side-effects of our decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always had a reputation as a business-friendly country.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this Bill, we might risk that reputation by again intervening with how contracts play out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It remains unclear whether there will be a third, a fourth and then, a fifth extension.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will articulate a long-term plan for our construction sector that clarifies these doubts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about how MND and the rest of Government can help the construction sector bounce back on its feet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This crisis is an opportunity for our construction firms to become more nimble.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than ever, they need to embrace automation, upskilling and other productivity-related initiatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The unfortunate reality of COVID-19 is that many companies have shut down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the painful months of circuit breaker and dorm lockdowns, many experienced workers did not manage to find new employers and were often repatriated rather than circulated back into our economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These were workers with experience living and working here.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They know the expectations, they know the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is more efficient to rehire them than to roll the dice with new workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there is no easy way for companies to find and hire these workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MND and other Ministries should work together to reduce the obstacles to rehiring such workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can also provide more help for companies to hire workers who want to remain in Singapore but whose company has decided to terminate their contracts and send them back to their home country.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A temporary scheme to reconnect employers with such workers will be much appreciated by workers and employers, and it will help our economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   COVID-19 has dealt a severe blow to our construction industry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to developers and their employees, related suppliers, contractors and the blue-collar construction workers, even building owners, buyers, sellers and tenants have been affected.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many Singaporeans who anticipated their new HDB flats have had to delay moving into their new homes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Bill seeks to provide viable and reasonable solutions for all affected stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This 122-day duration is longer than the three months' circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most main contractors will issue a bankers' guarantee to the developer in order to perform contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Doing so will only heap additional burdens upon troubled SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MND work with relevant commerce chambers and associations, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to inform the industry and banks here?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One way to prevent similar delays from happening in the future is to reduce reliance on foreign labour and supplies coming from overseas by improving productivity and upscaling domestic manufacturing capabilities to produce more Precast Concrete Building Components.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe the Government is already working on these changes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To prepare myself for the debate on this Bill, I had a chat with a successful "TowKay" (business owner), to understand more about the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I jokingly asked Mr Lee, "You are already so wealthy, despite the on-going challenges.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why are you still going after every tender and cent?" His reply was, "I have many mouths to feed." Indeed, like our Government, many local construction owners have a strong sense of responsibility to take care of their employees, many of whom are sole breadwinners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe the Government will work with the industry and address the concerns so that our country’s infrastructure development will not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The freezing of borders and shutdowns in various countries have meant delays in supplies arriving from overseas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Locally, manpower constraints have been acute as it has been difficult to get workers from abroad, while workers located in Singapore have been prevented from working or delayed from working both by the general lockdown and safety measures as well as dormitory specific constraints.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Labour costs have also risen as employers compete with each other for the limited available manpower.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against hits backdrop, the Government’s interventions have provided an important lifeline for those in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Extensions of time have been given for performance of obligations, which is vital because liquidated damages may kick in otherwise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The rights to call performance bonds have been limited, and effectively, the legislation has prevented parties from penalising counterparties who cannot perform because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, I think this is a well thought through Bill that tries to carefully share the burden of the losses arising from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Absent legislation, I think it is likely to fall on the smaller players down the value chain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do have a few clarifications to ask the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One group that will suffer from delays in construction is the ultimate purchaser.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, the aim of the legislation is to share the costs and losses across the value chain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am interested to know how effectively this is being done in practice?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, while extensions of time are being given for project completion, payment is the lifeline of the construction sector and work is still expected to continue during this period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is the Government aware of companies in hardship because they are expected to continue to work but are unable to receive payments in the meantime as a result of this legislation?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will typically apply to the main contractors and others who may be sandwiched.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what will happen is the subcontractors who are below them, may be able to get extensions of time from delivering against their obligations; which means that the work the contractor higher up has to do to receive his payment, will not be complete.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But this contractor higher up the value chain may have to pay other sub-contractors who had done their work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am just curious whether any larger contractors or contractors at the middle of the value chain have been facing hardship and may face further hardship as a result of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If this is not done voluntarily, then, further legislative intervention may be necessary to address this issue – otherwise, it is the parties in the middle of the value chain that may crack under pressure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the points above, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They have raised a number of issues and let me address them.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the impacts of the reliefs and our considerations for extension.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The sanctity of contract is fundamental for Singapore and a key aspect of the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, this is not a decision we take lightly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In this exceptional circumstance, we need to intervene to safeguard and preserve the capacity of our Built Environment sector, by supporting the entire value chain.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The industry has also consistently provided feedback to us that the on-going moratorium on legal proceedings during the current COVID-19 pandemic has proven very useful in helping the sector focus on staying on its feet.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Ng also asked about the percentage of parties that have been able to resolve their differences amicably and in a beneficial manner.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This suggests to us that the majority were able to come to some satisfactory compromise on their own about contractual obligations affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The relief provided under this Act, provides a framework for conversations to happen so that firms can amicably settle their differences and move the projects forward if they can do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about Part 3 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These are exceptional measures that temporarily suspended creditors' rights to provide breathing room for financially distressed debtors to negotiate with creditors and pursue next steps, including for personal bankruptcy, the individual voluntary arrangement and debt repayment scheme; for corporate insolvency, out-of-court work-about schemes of arrangement, judicial management and simplified Insolvency Programme; for sole proprietorships and partnerships, the Sole Proprietor and Partnership scheme.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Such exceptional measures should be carefully monitored because the measures also affect creditors and therefore, flow of credit to other businesses.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There has been no significant increase in number of personal bankruptcy and corporate insolvency applications, comparing the figures for applications pre-COVID-19 and the post lapse of Part 3 measures in October 2020.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have been monitoring the situation and we will continue to monitor it.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Louis Ng brought up the immediate challenge of manpower shortage faced by the industry.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And I agree with both Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Louis Ng that beyond the temporary relief measures, it is important to address this situation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To alleviate the current labour shortage in the construction industry, we are working closely with MOM and MOH to progressively increase the number of incoming workers, but in a safe way to minimise the risk of COVID-19 transmission in our dormitories and into our wider community.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Indeed, there are many operational challenges that we need to overcome to ensure reliable testing overseas.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we are actively in discussion with industry partners, including the Singapore Contractors Association Limited, or SCAL, and we are looking at how we can enable and establish better upstream processes to enhance pre-departure testing for workers in source countries.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I also agree with Mr Ng that there is value to retain experienced workers in Singapore as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, as Mr Kwek has pointed out, there are also workers who want to go back to their families and there are indeed workers who went home and could not return or would not like to return.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But however, we are trying to keep as many of our workers in Singapore here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In this regard, SCAL, with the support of MOM and BCA, has set up a Manpower Exchange, or SCMX for short, to facilitate a change of employer for construction workers, for workers whose contracts with their existing employers have either expired or terminated.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will help us retain the experienced workers who want to remain in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On Mr Ng's suggestion to facilitate the re-hiring of workers who have returned to their home countries and want to come back to Singapore to work, we are very pleased to have them back in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And employers know who they are and have applied for them to re-enter into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The constraint now and the challenge we are facing is how to allow these workers to come back, to re-enter Singapore in sufficient numbers to meet the industry's manpower needs, while minimising COVID-19 importation risks, so as to safeguard public health.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are working closely with MOM and MOH on these aspects.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Vikram Nair rightly pointed out that cashflow is the lifeline of the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: BCA monitors the progress payments in the industry closely and receives frequent feedback from key developers and contractors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is also why we need to extend the reliefs under the Act so firms do not get engaged in long-drawn litigations at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: During the circuit breaker period, most works were suspended and contractors received no progress payments.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: What we did to facilitate the cashflow was for Government agencies – and some private developers have also followed suit – to provide advance payment to help contractors tide through this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government has also provided financial support, including waivers and rebates of the foreign worker levy, and subsidies for Rostered Routine Testing, or RRT for short.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Vikram Nair also asked about co-sharing of additional costs for delays due to COVID-19 under Part 8B and how easy it is for such prolongation costs to be shared.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To facilitate such claims, BCA and SCAL have jointly developed a claims template and detailed guidelines, which are available on BCA's website.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In addition, BCA has also been working with SCAL and other Trade Associations and Chambers, to streamline the claims process.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes introducing an accepted method to estimate the delays to projects due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to work with the various stakeholders, including SCAL and other Government agencies to expedite the claims process.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Lastly, under Part 8B, contractors can also seek recourse for cost-sharing amounts that are due but not paid, through the existing adjudication mechanism under the Security of Payment Act, or SOPA, which the industry is very familiar with.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Don Wee suggested that we inform the industry and banks on extension of period where developers are prevented from calling on the performance bonds of contractors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Wee may be pleased to know that the provisions for deferment of call of performance bonds is already provided for in the Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MND and BCA have been in close contact with the industry and we have updated the industry on extension of arrangement under the Act, including through a press release.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Don Wee also brought up the impact on the construction industry and it has affected home-buyers whose premises under construction have been delayed and who have to make alternative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And Mr Vikram Nair has also asked about the extent to which these purchasers have been affected.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The number of purchasers seeking reimbursement after Part 8C comes into operation in a few months will depend on the number of projects delayed and whether developers need and choose to tap on this relief.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is in the interest of developers for projects to be completed in a timely manner without having to tap on the relief.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Currently, based on updates from developers for projects expected to be completed in 2021, most are still on track to meet their respective dates of delivery of possession.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have also been encouraging developers who are unable to meet the date of delivery to first discuss with their purchasers and come to a workable and mutually agreeable arrangement, as this may result in a better outcome for both parties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Don Wee asked why four months, why 122 days.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Should a developer need further relief for the delivery date to be extended by more than 122 days, they can apply for an assessor's determination on the length of construction delay, that is, to a material extent, caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Don Wee also asked about whether this relief will be applied to developments where HDB is the developer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This allows for co-sharing of such costs between the developer and purchaser.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And if there is any dispute over reimbursement, both parties can seek an assessor's determination.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To also to reply Mr Don Wee's query regarding the assessors, similar to Part 2, the assessors making the determinations under Part 8C will be professionals with qualifications and working experience in the relevant fields, such as law, accountancy, finance, or building and construction.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There will be mechanisms put in place to ensure that assessors declare any conflict of interest upfront.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked why Part 8C is not in operation yet and why amendments to Part 8C are being made at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There are many urgent Parts to the amendment that we moved in November last year, including Part 8, Part 8A and Part 8B and we have made sure that those Parts are in operation as quickly as we can.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For Part 8C, we have been in active discussion over the last few months with the industry and partners that will run and operationalise the relief framework.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And we are making amendments now as we incorporate their feedback in preparation for the operationalisation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We aim to streamline the process and help it be implemented more smoothly and more efficiently, given that it will be in effect for a longer period of time as compared to other reliefs under the Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, developers will be able to tap on it after it comes into operation in a few months and purchasers will be able to seek reimbursement then.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Lim also asked how we will address the issue of fairness, given that legal representation will be not be allowed as a default under the assessor framework and she spoke in support of it.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As with other Parts of the Act, the assessor mechanism is designed to provide for a quick and effective practical solution to disputes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Lim raised the concern that a company may be represented by a legally trained employee.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But there is a difference if you say that no one who is legally trained should come before an assessor.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: What if the individual purchaser himself is legally trained?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The point is that the assessment framework weeks to give relief on very simple facts when there would otherwise be no relief.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the first instance, we hope to minimise the need for them to come before an assessor to seek determination.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.00 pm until 4.20 pm.
